metadata.title: Reading for Change: Performance and Engagement across Countries (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD/PISA 2000 monograph reports results for a target population of 15-year-olds assessed in schools across 32 participating countries, using a complex sampling design with rigorous rules to ensure representativeness within each country. The report states that principals’ school questionnaire responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, but it does not provide the student-level sampling weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures. Because this is a descriptive and multilevel regression reporting framework rather than an ML prediction study, the manuscript does not document how analysts should apply student sampling weights in the international database. For replication with PISA microdata, analysts should use the standard PISA 2000 student sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the OECD PISA database/technical documentation to account for stratification and clustering; however, the exact weight variable names are not specified in the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The provided excerpt does not describe any plausible-value (PV) generation/combining procedure for cognitive outcomes, nor does it report a missing-data handling method for the analytic models. This monograph primarily presents descriptive statistics (means, distributions, percentiles) and multilevel regression results using PISA reading literacy scales derived from IRT-based scaling, without detailing PV-specific estimation steps in the text shown. Missing data are discussed only at a high level via reporting conventions (e.g., categories n.a/m/x in tables), but no explicit imputation/deletion rule is documented here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report targets 15-year-olds enrolled in educational institutions at the time of assessment, excluding 15-year-olds not enrolled in school. It also notes that countries could exclude up to 5% of the target population, including students with mental, emotional or physical disabilities that would prevent them from performing in the assessment situation and non-native language speakers with less than one year of instruction in the language of assessment. For the descriptive chapters, the Netherlands is excluded from analyses in Chapter 4 due to a low initial response rate (27%), though it is included in later chapters (5-7). Beyond these stated exclusions, the excerpt does not specify additional analytic subsample filters (e.g., complete-case rules) for the multilevel models.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD monograph reports descriptive and model-based results from PISA 2000, where reading literacy was the major domain (written tasks administered in schools to 15-year-olds). The reading construct is operationalized via an IRT scaling approach over 141 reading tasks, summarized on a composite reading literacy scale (mean 500, SD 100) and five subscales (three aspects: retrieving information, interpreting texts, reflection & evaluation; two formats: continuous and non-continuous texts). The report emphasizes cross-country comparisons of mean performance, score distributions across proficiency levels, and inequality within countries using 90th–10th percentile gaps. It also constructs an index of reading engagement (time spent reading for enjoyment, interest/attitudes, and diversity of reading materials) and examines associations between engagement and reading achievement, including interactions with parents’ occupational status. Methodologically, the excerpt does not document PV combining or missing-data handling procedures, and it does not present ML model performance metrics; instead, it uses multilevel regression frameworks to separate within-school and between-school relationships.
